$schema_doc: Each Instagram carousel post is one object. The schedule-tweets skill picks up the first post with status='pending' and posts it to Instagram with the slides attached in order. Status flow: 'draft' (slides not yet generated) -> 'pending' (slides ready, queued) -> 'posting' (mid-flight) -> 'posted' (live) -> 'failed'. IG carousel constraints: 2-10 slides per post, single shared caption up to 2,200 chars, up to 30 hashtags total. Each slide is a separate image (1:1 or 4:5; aspect ratio must be uniform across the carousel). The slides array must have between 2 and 10 entries before status can be 'pending'. The hashtags array is stored separately so it can be appended to the caption or posted as the first comment. The source_post field links to the YT post the carousel was repurposed from. likes and comments are populated when results are captured (default 7 days post-posting).

$post_schema.caption: <full caption text, <= 2,200 chars; hook on first line>

slides.slide_text: <text rendered on the slide, for traceability>

posts.caption:
Bitcoin does about 7 transactions per second.

$KAS just hit 5,700.

That's 800x the throughput on a fair-launched proof-of-work chain. Here's why this number matters more than almost anyone in crypto is talking about.

Bitcoin's whole reason for existing was to be peer-to-peer electronic cash. The 2008 Satoshi white paper is explicit. The pitch was a payment system that doesn't need banks; money that moves at the speed money needs to move.

It doesn't.

7 transactions per second across the entire global network. Confirmation times in tens of minutes when congested. Fees that spike to $20+ during high activity.

Try paying for a coffee with that. Try sending payroll to a thousand employees. Try running a global remittance flow. The network physically cannot handle it.

Now look at $KAS.

5,700 TPS. Block times measured in milliseconds. Fees that round to zero.

The chain that can do what Bitcoin promised in 2008 wasn't built by Satoshi. It was built by someone who looked at Bitcoin's structural limits and decided to fix them, while keeping what made Bitcoin valuable: proof of work, fair launch, no premine, no insiders.

Throughput matters because no asset can be money if you can't move it fast enough.

Gold isn't money in the modern sense. It's a settlement layer. Bitcoin is currently in the same category. The actual transactions of daily commerce can't run on it.

5,700 TPS opens doors Bitcoin physically cannot:

Real merchant adoption. Not "we accept Bitcoin" with a 30-minute confirmation wait, but actual payment terminals at credit-card swipe speed.

Micropayments. The small-dollar transactions crushed by gas fees on slower chains.

Global remittance flows. Workers sending money home without losing 10% to Western Union.

On-chain commerce at consumer scale.

The bull case for $KAS isn't "it might replace Bitcoin."

The bull case is: Bitcoin can't do its own job. $KAS can.

posts.caption:
October 2025 wasn't the cycle top.

It was a midcycle top so weak it didn't even reach average power law.

The 2013 and 2019 midcycle tops both blew past it. The actual cycle top is still ahead.

Most of crypto Twitter is mourning a top that didn't actually happen. Let me walk you through why.

First, definitions.

A midcycle top is the local high that prints partway through a cycle, not the cycle top itself. Every prior cycle has had one.

Look at 2013. $BTC ran from around $13 in January to about $259 in early April. It peaked, sold off ~85% to roughly $50 by July, then ran all the way to $1,150 by year-end. That April peak wasn't the cycle top. It was the midcycle top.

The 2019 setup was the same shape, just scaled up.

$BTC ran from ~$3,200 in December 2018 to about $13,800 in June 2019. Then it sold off into the COVID wick at ~$3,800 in March 2020. The actual cycle top didn't print until November 2021 at roughly $69,000.

What both of those midcycle tops have in common: they blew well past average power law.

Average power law isn't a magic indicator. It's the regression line drawn through the middle of $BTC's lifetime price action. Past midcycle tops cleared it convincingly. That's how you tell a real local high from sideways noise.

October 2025 didn't reach it.

The "top" everyone is now grieving peaked below average power law. By any prior pattern, that's not a cycle top. That's a local high inside a sideways structure.

If October had even matched the 2019 midcycle overshoot, $BTC would have printed somewhere north of $200k.

The four-year cycle zombies grieving October as the top are extrapolating from a midcycle high that didn't even break trend.

The actual cycle top is still ahead. When it prints, it'll be well above average power law, like every previous one. Save this for the next time someone tells you the cycle is over.

slides.slide_text: October 2025 wasn't the cycle top. It did not reach average power law.
The 2013 midcycle peaked at $259. The actual top came at $1,150 eight months later.
The 2019 midcycle peaked at $13,800. The actual top hit $69K two and a half years later.
Every real midcycle blew past average power law. October 2025 peaked below it.
When does the actual cycle top print?

posts.caption:
The four-year cycle didn't break.

It never existed.

What people called "the cycle" was three macro variables happening to line up. And the people still acting like it's real just cost $BTC roughly $15k of price.

For about a decade, three things lined up almost perfectly with the Bitcoin halving calendar:

1. The business cycle. PMI expanded, then contracted.
2. Money printing. QE turned on, then off.
3. Interest rates. The Fed cut, then hiked.

Every "crypto cycle" since 2014 rode the same wave. People credited the halving as the cause. The halving was incidental.

The proof is in the bears. Every prior crypto bear (2014, 2018, 2022) maps cleanly onto PMI rolling over, QE ending, and rates rising.

The 2014 bear got blamed on Mt. Gox. Underneath, the Fed taper was running. The 2018 bear got blamed on the ICO bust. Underneath, the Fed lifted rates from 1.25% to 2.5% and ran QT. The 2022 bear got blamed on Luna and FTX. Underneath, the fastest hiking cycle in 40 years was happening.

Three different surface stories. One identical macro setup underneath.

This time the three variables didn't line up.

PMI is expanding. QE is running. Rates are coming down, not up.

The conditions that created every previous "crypto winter" simply aren't present.

But the four-year cycle zombies didn't notice. They saw the calendar (year four after a halving). They saw a shutdown-driven dip. They assumed the bear had arrived. Long-term holders started distributing. Sell pressure compounded. Down we went.

The dip wasn't macro. It wasn't structural. It was a self-fulfilling prophecy from people convinced of a cycle that never existed.

If they hadn't dumped, $BTC would be at ~$95k right now instead of $80k. The current price is the cost of acting on a dead theory.

Once you see it as macro coincidence, you can't unsee it. Save this for the next time someone tells you the cycle is over.

If the cycle is dead, what is the new framework?

posts.caption:
Every previous crypto bear lined up with macro tightening.

Rates up. QT. PMI down.

This "bear" is happening with QE running and PMI expanding. The opposite of every prior one.

Either we just rewrote how crypto cycles work, or this isn't a bear at all.

Three previous bears, three identical macro setups underneath, and why the present setup doesn't fit any of them.

2014 bear. Surface story: post-Mt. Gox unwind. Real story: the Fed taper. QE3 ended in December 2014. PMI rolled through 2015. $BTC drained from about $1,150 to roughly $170. The headlines blamed the exchange collapse. The macro did most of the lifting.

2018 bear. Surface story: ICO bust. Real story: rate hikes. The Fed lifted from 1.25% to 2.5% over 12 months. QT was running simultaneously. PMI peaked mid-2018 and rolled. $BTC went from about $19,500 down to $3,200.

2022 bear. Surface story: Luna and FTX. Real story: the fastest hiking cycle in 40 years. The Fed went from 0% to 5.5% in 18 months. QT was running. PMI contracted. $BTC went from roughly $69,000 to $15,500.

Three bears. Three different surface stories. One identical macro setup underneath: tightening plus contraction.

Now look at the present.

PMI: expanding.
QE: running.
Rates: coming down, not up.

Pull a chart of any of those three prior crypto bears and overlay these conditions. They don't fit. None of the boxes that defined the past three bears are checked. Not one.

So either we just witnessed the first crypto bear in history that happened during the opposite macro setup, or what looked like a bear was actually a panic in a bull setup, driven by people still acting on the old playbook.

Occam's razor picks the second one.

The macro behind crypto is doing the opposite of what most accounts will admit. Save this for the next time someone tells you the cycle is over.

posts.caption:
The 50-week SMA breakdown wasn't real.

200-week SMA was barely wicked on a single Thursday. No weekly close at or below it.

Technically, this isn't even crypto winter. People behaved like it was.

The cost of acting on belief instead of charts is roughly $15k per Bitcoin.

First, definitions. "Crypto winter" has a specific meaning. It's the period after $BTC closes weekly below the 200-week moving average, traditionally for sustained weeks. The 200-week SMA is the long-term trend line. Closing below it is what "the long-term structure broke" actually means in chart terms. It's not vibes. It's a defined event.

What actually happened in October:

$BTC wicked toward the 200-week SMA on a single Thursday. It didn't close at or below it on the weekly. Not even once. By the strict definition, the structural break never happened. The trend held.

But people behaved as if the break had already happened. Long-term holders, the cohort that's supposed to weather these moments and accumulate into them, distributed into the dip instead. The on-chain data is unambiguous: LTH supply dropped through October and November.

That's not what smart positioning looks like. That's what panic looks like.

Ill-advised long-term holders sold a bear they invented in their own heads. Not because the chart broke. Because they thought it would.

Here's what their behavior cost: $BTC at roughly $80k right now instead of $95k. That ~$15k delta is a tax on people who acted on a thesis their own charts weren't confirming. It's also a discount for whoever didn't sell.

The lesson is small and uncomfortable.

Read your own charts before you act on a narrative. The 50-week SMA "breakdown" wasn't a breakdown. The 200-week SMA "test" wasn't a structural break. Crypto winter wasn't here.

It was always belief acting on incomplete reading. Save this for the next time someone tells you the cycle is over.
